    THEON RANCHES, LP, DANIEL AND KATHRYN VOSS, AND D & M DAVIS LAND
              AND CATTLE, L.P.’S POST HEARING INITIAL BRIEF

         Theon Ranches, LP, Daniel and Kathryn Voss, and D&M Davis Land and Cattle, L.P.

(Theon-Voss and D&M Davis) 1 hereby file their Post Hearing Initial Brief, and respectfully urge

the Administrative Law Judges (ALJs) to recommend that the Commission approve the

Applicants’ proposed Route 894, and in support thereof show as follows:


I.       INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY

         Theon-Voss and D&M Davis expresses its sincere thanks for the ALJs’ attention to this

case, their attention to the parties’ arguments, testimonies, and briefing.

         Nearly every landowner who participated in this proceeding argued that the 765 kV

transmission line proposed by Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (Oncor) and LCRA

Transmission Services Corporation (LCRA TSC) (collectively, Applicants) would ruin their land

and way of life. For some, the line threatens ranching, hunting, family heritage, wildlife habitat,


1
     For ease of identification Theon-Voss and D&M Davis were designated Intervenor No. 40 in this proceeding.

SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                            3                  Theon-Voss and D&M Davis’s
PUC Docket No. 59475                                            Post Hearing Initial Brief – Intervenor #40
 or rural solitude. For others, the line threatens planned development, including commercial and

residential investment.

        But the Legislature has already made a policy judgment that Texas must develop the

transmission infrastructure necessary to serve rapidly growing electric demand, including in

regions affected by Permian Basin electrification and large-load growth. House Bill 5066, effective

June 13, 2023, directed the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission) and the Electric

Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) process for reliability plans in areas with transmission

needs, including the Permian Basin, and required implementation planning for necessary

transmission service improvements. 2

        Thus, this proceeding pits private property rights against the energy infrastructure required

to serve a growing Texas economy. Unless the Commission denies the Application or the

Legislature changes course, a line will be built. And whatever route is selected, the record

demonstrates that it will fragment private property. The route will definitely affect rural

agricultural land, ranch land, undeveloped land, land in various stages of development, riparian

areas, and rivers, and possibly park and recreational lands.

        Given this reality, the Commission’s routing criteria play an important role for selecting a

path for a new transmission line. Crucially, a landowner not wanting the line on or near their

property, is not a differentiating factor in selecting a route for the line. Precisely because of that

single unifying feature amongst the landowners, the Commission adopted the routing criteria

shown in its CCN Application form, and has over the years through its orders, refined those

criteria. The Commission’s task in this proceeding is not to select a route that is free of impact, but




2
    Tex. H.B. 5066, 88th Leg., R.S. (2023).

SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                      4                 Theon-Voss and D&M Davis’s
PUC Docket No. 59475                                     Post Hearing Initial Brief – Intervenor #40
 instead to select a route, when evaluated from end to end, that best meets the statutory and rule-

based criteria found in PURA § 37.056(c)(4) and 16 Texas Administrative Code (TAC) § 25.101.

        Most parties, including the Applicants, look to the Commission’s routing criteria and

invariably point to a route or routes they believe “best meets” those criteria. And the Applicants

did no differently in this proceeding identifying Route 894 as the route out of 122 potential routes

that best meets the Commission’s routing criteria, that is, the “Best Meets” route. 3

        Theon-Voss and D&M Davis agree. The Applicants’ objective is to obtain approval to

construct a line that can be built in a timely manner. Although the workings of rate-of-return

regulation incentivize the Applicants – or at least Oncor – to build the costliest line, the Applicants

did not select the longest or most expensive route, instead they selected Route 894. Here, the

evidence presented by the Applicants and affirmed by Theon-Voss and D&M Davis’s expert

witness Mr. James W. Daniel, 4 supports the ALJs giving the Applicants’ selection meaningful

weight. 5 At bottom, the Applicants’ selection reflects a route-wide balancing of the Commission’s

criteria, not a link-by-link effort to favor any individual landowner.

        Route 894 is not the perfect route. Route 894, like most, if not all, of the routes affects farm

land in rural Texas, undeveloped, undisturbed, pristine ranch lands, land developments in various

stages of development in urban Texas, riparian areas, and the Colorado river. But the Commission

does not select a transmission line route by simply isolating individual links and asking whether

 another link in the study area might perform better on a single metric. Instead, the Commission

applies a holistic approach to selecting a route.

           The record shows that when applying such an end-to-end approach Route 894 compares

most favorably under the Commission’s routing criteria. At bottom, Route 894 best balances cost,

length, habitable structures, paralleling, environmental impacts, land use, and community values.

           Thus, Theon-Voss and D&M Davis urge the ALJs to recommend approval of Route 894

to the Commission. Alternatively, if the ALJs do not recommend approval of Route 894, the ALJs

should reject any route using Links B3, F42, or F43.

II.        JOINT APPLICATION

           Theon-Voss and D&M Davis are not addressing this issue in its initial brief.

VI.        ROUTE – BEST MEETS ROUTE

           A.      The applicable statutory and regulatory criteria require a holistic analysis
                   to determine which proposed route best meets such criteria.

           PURA § 37.056(c)(4) requires the Commission to consider, among other factors,

community values, recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic values, and environmental

integrity. 6 The Commission’s substantive rule, 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B), further requires

consideration of routing factors, engineering constraints, and costs, so that the line is “routed to


6
       PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A)-(D).

SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                        6                Theon-Voss and D&M Davis’s
PUC Docket No. 59475                                      Post Hearing Initial Brief – Intervenor #40
 the extent reasonable to moderate the impact on the affected community and landowners unless

grid reliability and security dictate otherwise.” 7 The routing factors include the extent to which

proposed routes parallel or utilize existing compatible rights-of-way, other compatible rights-of-

way, property lines, and other natural or cultural features. 8 The routing factors also include whether

the proposed routes conform with the policy of prudent avoidance. 9

           These factors are not applied by prioritizing one factor above all others. Instead, the

Commission’s task is to balance the applicable statutory and regulatory factors to determine which

proposed route best meets the criteria as a whole.

           In the current proceeding, parties that argued against particular links of Route 894

advocated for alternative routes that create equal or greater impacts elsewhere. 10 But a critique

focused on individual links is not a route-wide analysis. A route may contain individual links that

are not ideal and still be the route that best balances the Commission’s criteria overall. Conversely,

a route that avoids one party’s property may impose greater overall impacts when evaluated as a

whole.

           B.     Route 894 is the route that best meets the applicable statutory and
                  regulatory criteria when evaluated as a complete route.

           The Applicants are indifferent to which individual landowner ultimately bears the burden

of the line. Their objective is to construct the transmission line along the route approved by the

Commission. If ordered to build a longer or more expensive route, the Applicants will do so.

Indeed, under traditional rate-of-return principles higher capital investment would almost certainly

 increase the revenue requirement the Applicants – or at least Oncor – would ultimately recover

from ratepayers. Yet the Applicants did not select the longest or more expensive route.

         After a holistic analysis of the 122 proposed alternative routes, the Applicants “selected

Route 894 as the route that best addresses the requirements of PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A)-(D) and

16 TAC § 25.101.” 11 The Applicants derived their decision from a number of considerations.

Specifically, the Applicants identified Route 894 as the Best Meets route because Route 894:

             •    Is approximately 223.7 miles, which is 20.7 miles shorter than the longest filed

                  route;

             •    Has an estimated cost of $1,680,919,000, which is approximately 9.52% less costly

                  than the filed route with the most expensive transmission line cost;

             •    Has 85 habitable structures within 500 feet of the route centerline, which is 99 less

                  than the filed route with the highest number;

             •    Parallels existing compatible rights-of-way for approximately 43.9% of its length;

             •    Crosses only 162.8 miles of rangeland pasture;

             •    Crosses riparian areas for only 42.52 miles compared to the highest length of the

                  filed routes crossing riparian areas of 55.63 miles;

             •    Crosses no cross parks or recreational areas, does not have any parks or recreational

                  areas within 1,000 feet of its centerline, and has no miles of right-of-way (ROW)

                  within a foreground visual zone of any park/recreational area;

             •    Crosses only 0.16 miles of agricultural cropland with mobile irrigation systems

                  compared to the highest length of filed routes crossing agricultural cropland with

                  mobile irrigation systems of 0.72 miles;

     Applicants Exh. 1 – Application at 28, 1986.

PUC Docket No. 59475                                       Post Hearing Initial Brief – Intervenor #40
               •     Only has one known rare/unique plant potentially located within the proposed right-

                    of-way compared to the highest number of four;

              •     Crosses only 0.09 miles of known habitat of federally listed endangered or

                    threatened species;

              •     Has only three FAA-registered airports with a runway greater than 3,200 feet within

                    20,000 feet of the centerline;

              •     Has only three FAA-registered airports with no runway greater than 3,200 feet

                    within 10,000 feet of the centerline;

              •     Has only two private airstrips within 10,000 feet of the centerline;

              •     Has no heliports located within 5,000 feet of the centerline;

              •     Has no commercial AM radio transmitters located within 10,000 feet of the

                    centerline;

              •     Has only five microwave or other electronic installation within 2,000 feet of the

                    route centerline; and

              •     Has been judged to be feasible from an engineering perspective. 12

         Several intervenor witnesses provide independent support for the Applicants’ conclusion

that Route 894 best meets the applicable statutory and regulatory criteria. 13 In addition to the

intervenor witnesses supporting Route 894, Theon-Voss and D&M Davis’s expert, Mr. James W.

Daniel, also demonstrates that Route 894 performs the best overall under key routing criteria.

          The record establishes that Route 894 compares favorably across the Commission’s routing

criteria. As Mr. Daniel stated in his direct testimony, the EA used by the Applicants considers 35

factors and provides a “rigorous analysis of all potential transmission line routes based on the

Commission’s routing criteria . . . .” 14 Mr. Daniel also explained that, in his experience, the primary

factors typically considered most important in selecting a transmission route are “[l]ength of the

alternative route,” “[t]he alternative route’s estimated cost,” “[t]he portion of the alternative route

parallel to existing ROW and apparent property lines; and,” “[t]he number of habitable structures

within 500 feet of the ROW centerline for the alternative route.” 15 He further noted that these were

the first four factors in the Applicants’ Routing Memo, which “suggests that the Applicants also

considered these the top four route analysis factors.” 16

         Measured against these top four routing factors, Route 894 performs well. Mr. Daniel

testified that Route 894 is only 9.2 miles longer than the shortest route, has an estimated cost that

is only 2.73% more than the least expensive alternative route, has only 5 more habitable structures

than the routes with the least number of habitable structures, and has 43.9% of its length parallel

to existing compatible ROW. 17

         Although Route 894 is not the best route on every isolated factor, it performs favorably on

the four major factors that the Commission relies on in its analysis. And so, the ALJs should

recommend that the Commission select Route 894 as the Best Meets route.

          C.           Route 894 also performs well when compared against many other routes,
                      including those that use Links F42, F43, and B3.

         Route 894 also compares favorably against the routes that impact Theon-Voss and D&M

Davis’s properties along Links F42, F43, and B3, which include routes 322, 366, 376, 381, 382,

910, 911, 913, 914, 915, 916, 1162, and 1164 (collectively, the Opposed Routes). 18

         The record shows that the Opposed Routes would have “a detrimental impact on cattle

ranching operations and/or land development opportunities,” are “more expensive than the

Applicants’ recommended route 894, and many other routes,” are “longer than the Applicants’

recommended route,” have “more habitable structures within 500 feet of the route’s centerline,”

and, with only two exceptions, have “a longer portion of their route that is not parallel to existing

compatible ROWs” than Route 894, which “will likely result in more fragmentation of previously

undisturbed land.” 19

                      1.    Routes that impact Theon-Voss and D&M Davis’s properties would
                            be detrimental to cattle ranching operations and undermine
                            development opportunities.

         The Voss family owns cattle ranches located in the Eastern portion of the study area. 20

Several of the routes would fragment these Voss family properties, including routes 322, 366, 376,

381, 382, 910, 911, 913, 914, 915, 916, 1162, and 1164. 21

         As Mr. Daniel explains, property fragmentation is “detrimental to cattle ranching during

the construction and maintenance of the transmission line and ROW and when maintaining

pastureland.” 22 A transmission line has the potential to “reduce the amount of vegetation available

 for grazing of cattle not only because of the width of the easement, but also the use of herbicides”

while “vegetation-management practices will impact the quality of forage available to graze

cattle.” 23 Mr. Daniel further testifies that “the transmission towers will impede the maintenance of

the land” and interfere with the “ability to locate working facilities on their land.” 24 Finally, the

transmission line would increase the risk of cattle escaping from the properties. 25 Mr. Daniel’s

testimony stands unrefuted.

         The record also demonstrates that because the properties owned by Theon-Voss and D&M

Davis are all located near the I-35 corridor north of Georgetown, Texas, “Theon-Voss and D&M

Davis will both have opportunities for the sale and/or development of their properties.” 26 This

makes sense when considering that “Georgetown has been recognized as one of the fastest growing

cities in Texas.” 27 In fact, “the Voss family has received preliminary-plat approvals from

Williamson County to develop their land impacted by Link F42” while the property owned by

D&M Davis is “primed for development.” 28 Ultimately, “[i]f the approved transmission line route

crosses or borders their properties, or is in the vicinity of their properties, this will decrease the

value of their property and reduce or eliminate the ability to develop the property.”

         The Commission has articulated a clear standard that future development may be

considered in a CCN transmission line proceeding when the development has progressed beyond

a speculative plan. In Docket No. 57648, the Commission rejected a Proposal for Decision that

evidence to show the future development plans had been initiated. 29 Notably, the Commission did

question as “whether future development that could be affected by a proposed route has been

initiated in some readily observable or measurable way on that route.” 30

          Theon-Voss and D&M Davis’s properties meet this standard. The Voss family’s

preliminary-plat approvals from Williamson County, included in the record as the “Headwaters

Preliminary Plat,” 31 demonstrate the existence of a readily observable and measurable step in the

development process. Similarly, the Commission should also consider the strong development

potential of D&M Davis’s property. The fact that property is located along the I-35 corridor north

of one of the fastest growing cities in Texas and that Rock Bluff Ranch, the property immediately

south of D&M Davis’s property, is currently undergoing its own development process 32 together

with the Davis Ranch/City of Georgetown Plan 33 provide record evidence that the future

development of D&M Davis’s property has been initiated.

        Taken together, the factors discussed above demonstrate that Route 894 is an overall

balanced route. It is relatively short, low in cost, low in affected habitable structures, and

reasonable on paralleling compatible ROW. By contrast, the Opposed Routes impose higher cost,

greater length, more habitable structures, and greater fragmentation concerns while also burdening

Theon-Voss and D&M Davis properties with avoidable ranching impacts and property

devaluation.

       Thus, the record evidence demonstrates that the ALJs should recommend that the

Commission approve Route 894 as the Best Meets route.

         Theon-Voss and D&M Davis expresses its sincere thanks for the ALJs' attention to this

case, their attention to the parties' arguments, testimonies, and briefing.

         Nearly every landowner who participated in this proceeding argued that the 765 kV

transmission line proposed by Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (Oncor) and LCRA

Transmission Services Corporation (LCRA TSC) (collectively, Applicants) would min their land

and way of life. For some, the line threatens ranching, hunting, family heritage, wildlife habitat,

        But the Legislature has already made a policy judgment that Texas must develop the

        Given this reality, the Commission's routing criteria play an important role for selecting a

shown in its CCN Application form, and has over the years through its orders, refined those

criteria. The Commission' s task in this proceeding is not to select a route that is free of impact, but

           A.      The applicable statutory and regulatory criteria require a holistic analysis
                   to determine which proposed route best meets such criteria.

           PURA § 37.056(c)(4) requires the Commission to consider, among other factors,

community values, recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic values, and environmental

integrity.6 The Commission's substantive rule, 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B), further requires

consideration of routing factors, engineering constraints, and costs, so that the line is "routed to

grid reliability and security dictate otherwise." 7 The routing factors include the extent to which

proposed routes parallel or utilize existing compatible rights-of-way, other compatible rights-of-

way, property lines, and other natural or cultural features. 8 The routing factors also include whether

the proposed routes conform with the policy of prudent avoidance. 9

           These factors are not applied by prioritizing one factor above all others. Instead, the

Commission's task is to balance the applicable statutory and regulatory factors to determine which

proposed route best meets the criteria as a whole.

           In the current proceeding, parties that argued against particular links of Route 894

advocated for alternative routes that create equal or greater impacts elsewhere. 10 But a critique

focused on individual links is not a route-wide analysis. A route may contain individual links that

are not ideal and still be the route that best balances the Commission's criteria overall. Conversely,

a route that avoids one party' s property may impose greater overall impacts when evaluated as a

whole.

           The Applicants are indifferent to which individual landowner ultimately bears the burden

of the line. Their objective is to construct the transmission line along the route approved by the

Commission. If ordered to build a longer or more expensive route, the Applicants will do so.
